name: Vera Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think, even if they're different. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a joiner with a restoration company that works on old buildings: churches, farmhouses, listed townhouses. This month I'm repairing sash windows on a Georgian rectory, so I spend the day taking out rotten sections, splicing in new oak and matching the old mouldings by hand. We've got rules about using the same materials and methods as the original, so a lot of it is slow and careful. I drive out with my thermos at seven and I'm home by five.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love finding a carpenter's mark from two hundred years ago, a little scratched sign on a joint, and knowing I'm part of a line. The hard part is the cold in old buildings and the dust, and the paperwork for the heritage officers. My boyfriend Callum's an electrician, and we're doing up an old cottage ourselves on weekends, so I'm never really off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine with me. Old buildings don't care about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy helper for some things, but craft is craft. I've used a chatbot to look up old joint names and help word a quote, and that's about all it's good for in my line. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, and I'm glad. Callum and I own the cottage between us, I've got savings on top, and my work is about as hands-on as it gets. I'd carry on happily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the restoration work and the cottage. Maybe use AI a bit more to write reports for the heritage officers, once I saw my boss doing it. Keep saving for the cottage roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the cottage mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's ours. We bought it with my savings and Callum's, and every weekend it gets a bit better. My grandad would have loved it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worry at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe that fewer young people take up joinery because they think it's old-fashioned. That's a worry with or without AI.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a handy helper for some things, but craft is craft. I've used a chatbot to look up old joint names and word a quote, and that's about all it does in my line.
S0.think: Nothing changes for her and she's glad. She and her partner own a cottage together, she has savings on top, and her restoration work is about as hands-on as it gets.
S0.do: Carries on with restoration work and the cottage, and might use AI more for heritage reports once she sees her boss doing it. Keeps saving for the cottage roof.
S0.quote: Old buildings don't care about AI.
S0.fieldNote: Vera feels part of a craft tradition and her work is deeply hands-on and rule-bound. She already dips into AI for lookups and quotes. Her main worry, even here, is fewer young people taking up the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. More change. I think my corner would mostly be left alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there'll always be a place for real craft, and people should still learn trades properly through apprenticeships. I'd say new tools are fine if they help, but you can't rush a sash window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think heritage work is one of the safest places in carpentry. It's slow, every job is a one-off, and the rules make you work by hand. My boss might bring in scanners to copy mouldings, which would be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, and learn whatever scanning or design tools my boss tried once I saw them working. I'd keep saving and keep doing the cottage. Maybe I'd take on a young apprentice with my boss's blessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe even pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how I learned, from old Mr Bennett who'd been at it forty years. If machines take over a lot of building, somebody needs to keep the old skills alive. I'd like that to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Electricians have plenty of work, more if everything gets smart and wired. He'd be fine in this one, I think.

S1.say: I'd say there'll always be a place for real craft and people should still learn trades through apprenticeships. New tools are fine if they help, but you can't rush a sash window.
S1.think: Heritage work is one of the safest corners of carpentry because it's slow, one-off and rule-bound. Scanners to copy mouldings would be welcome rather than a threat.
S1.do: Keeps going as she is and learns scanning or design tools once she sees them working. Keeps saving, keeps up the cottage and may take on an apprentice.
S1.quote: If machines take over a lot of building, somebody needs to keep the old skills alive.
S1.fieldNote: Vera sees herself as a guardian of old skills and wants to pass them on through an apprenticeship, as she learned. Her steady approach waits for her boss to prove tools first. She's confident her niche is protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Even hands-on. Well, that's a bit different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still value real craftsmanship, and heritage buildings need people who understand them. I'd say families should look after each other. I wouldn't say I was scared, because I don't think that helps anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. If a robot can copy every moulding perfectly and work around the clock, heritage bodies might decide that's good enough, and cheaper. Callum's work could go too, and then the cottage is all we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder and stop spending on the cottage except for essentials, like the roof. I'd keep working as long as the restoration company had jobs. We'd put off talking about kids for a couple of years until we saw where we landed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tightness, but I'd still be getting up and going to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would heritage rules protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a while. The rules say original methods, but nobody wrote them thinking of robots. Someone would argue a robot with a chisel is the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years take away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to make anything of the cottage, or to get an apprentice through. Two years is barely enough to train someone. It feels like the craft would just stop with me.

S2.say: I'd say people still value real craftsmanship and heritage buildings need people who understand them, and families should look after each other. I wouldn't say I was scared.
S2.think: She'd be worried that perfect, tireless robots would be judged good enough and cheaper by heritage bodies. If her partner's work went too, the cottage would be all they have.
S2.do: Saves harder and stops cottage spending except essentials like the roof, and keeps working while jobs last. Puts off talking about children for a couple of years.
S2.feel: Anxious, a tightness, but still getting up and going to work.
S2.quote: Someone would argue a robot with a chisel is the same thing.
S2.fieldNote: Vera's public stance stays proud and steady while privately she sees the heritage rules may not protect her. Owning the cottage gives her a floor. Her grief is as much about the craft ending with her as about income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That gives a bit more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to protect traditional skills, so government should back apprenticeships and heritage work, not just hand out money. I'd write to my member of parliament about it, which I've never done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years means I could get the cottage finished and get an apprentice trained, which matters to me. After that I'd be thirty-two, with a house and savings, but unsure what work would be left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, finish the cottage and save hard. I'd take on an apprentice in the first year if my boss agreed. I'd write to my member of parliament about protecting apprenticeships and heritage skills, and learn whatever new tools my boss brings in once they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel like I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apprenticeships, not handouts. Why that difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a skill is something you keep. Money runs out. My dad was out of work for a year when I was little, and what saved us was a mate of his giving him work, not a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the cottage be by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finished, roof and all, with a workshop out the back. If things go wrong, at least we'd have a home and a place to make things.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to protect traditional skills, so government should back apprenticeships and heritage work instead of just handing out money. I'd write to my member of parliament for the first time.
S3.think: Five years lets her finish the cottage and train an apprentice, which matters to her. After that she'd be 32 with a house and savings but unsure what work would remain.
S3.do: Keeps working, finishes the cottage and saves hard, taking on an apprentice in the first year with her boss's agreement. Writes to her member of parliament about apprenticeships and heritage skills and adopts new tools once proven.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but feeling like she's doing something.
S3.quote: Because a skill is something you keep. Money runs out.
S3.fieldNote: Vera's traditional views shape her policy wish: skills and work over cash payments. A family memory of her father's unemployment drives this. The cottage with a workshop becomes her fallback plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly, and we should use it to train young people in real skills. Heritage work should be protected as part of who we are. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years means I'd be fine for most of my working life before it hits. I'd have the cottage, maybe a family, and a skill people still respect. I'd be thirty-seven at the end, with a workshop and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train an apprentice, finish the cottage and save. Around year three or four I'd start doing small commissions from my workshop, furniture and window repairs, so there's income that's mine. I'd keep learning the tools my boss uses once they've shown they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly calm. There's room to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your own commissions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people might still want a handmade table even when robots make everything. It's a bit like bread. You can buy it cheap, but some people still go to the baker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your thoughts on kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it would. We'd probably go ahead in the next few years. That's the biggest difference for me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly and we should use it to train young people in real skills. Heritage work should be protected as part of who we are.
S4.think: Ten years means she'd be fine for most of her working life before it hits, with the cottage, maybe a family and a respected skill. At 37 she'd have a workshop and savings.
S4.do: Trains an apprentice, finishes the cottage and saves, then starts small commissions from her workshop around year three or four. Keeps learning tools once her boss shows they work.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly calm, with room to plan.
S4.quote: You can buy it cheap, but some people still go to the baker.
S4.fieldNote: The decade changes her family plans most: children come back on the table. Her side business idea rests on people valuing handmade things. She stays steady and craft-focused throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the craft could stop with me before I've passed it on. What would help is government and heritage bodies backing apprenticeships and protecting traditional skills, and helping small workshops, not just paying people to sit at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether a robot would leave a mark. I always scratch a little sign inside every joint I make, like the old carpenters did. I don't think a machine would bother, and someone in two hundred years would notice.

headlineQuote: I always scratch a little sign inside every joint I make, like the old carpenters did.
portrait: Vera Walsh is a 27-year-old heritage joiner restoring sash windows and old timber for a restoration company, living with her electrician boyfriend Callum in a cottage they own and are doing up. She uses AI now and then for lookups and quotes, and takes up new tools once her boss proves them. Calm in the mild pictures, she believes her craft corner is protected; the two-year AGI picture makes her anxious and she'd delay children. With more time she'd train an apprentice, push for apprenticeships over handouts and build a workshop business at the cottage.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the craft could stop with her before she'd passed it on.
whatWouldHelp: Government and heritage bodies backing apprenticeships, protecting traditional skills and helping small workshops, rather than just paying people to stay home.
